paras: The threatened lynching of Doc Wilson took place in March 1881, when a mob reportedly organized in Macon, Georgia, to lynch Wilson, a young Black barber accused of killing a young Macon man, James Tinley. Officers who had brought Wilson back from Florida lodged him in the Atlanta jail instead, and no attack on him was reported. He was tried for murder in Macon in December 1881, in a case a correspondent said had stirred more feeling than any other before the court.

On a Monday night, February 7, 1881, James Tinley was shot through the heart in a Macon bar-room, and Wilson, described as a barber and barkeeper, escaped. Wilson's friends said Tinley had drawn a knife, while Tinley's friends said he was a peaceable man who carried none; a knife Wilson's brother Eugene produced turned out to bear the accused's own initials. According to the Macon Telegraph, Wilson later said he had run to the jail to give himself up but fled when he saw a "large and excited crowd" gathering at the scene.

Rewards for his arrest reached $450, including $250 from J. J. Tinley and $100 from Governor Colquitt. Wilson's friends were quoted as saying he would stand trial in six months but not amid the "excitement and prejudice against him," and the Telegraph urged that he be captured and tried speedily.

In early March, Sheriff Thebald of Chattahoochee County captured Wilson at Apalachicola, Florida, as he was about to board a lumber vessel bound for Boston, and sent him up the river toward Columbus in irons. Bibb County Sheriff Wescott, Police Chief John Hurley and Solicitor General Hardeman left Macon for Columbus to take charge of him, and Georgia papers said he would be held in the Atlanta jail "for safe keeping." An Atlanta dispatch dated March 9 said Wilson was brought to Atlanta that day and jailed because a mob had organized in Macon to lynch him. The coverage gives no size, leaders or actions for the mob.

Wilson was returned to Macon by early June; according to the Atlanta Constitution's Macon correspondent, a crowd filled the depot on his arrival and Sheriff Westcott hurried him from the train to the jail. The same report said Wilson's "colored friends" had raised a sum for his defense. His murder trial was set for December 12, and by December 15 testimony had closed after Wilson made a statement claiming self-defense. No verdict appears in the coverage, and no one was reported arrested for organizing the mob.

Most of the coverage concerned the killing and the manhunt rather than the mob. A Macon wire offering a $100 reward ran on February 10 and 11 in Washington, Lancaster, Richmond, Knoxville and Savannah, with the victim's name variously printed Tinley and Finley; the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer headed it "Negro Murderer at Large." The Savannah Morning News, summarizing the Macon Telegraph, called Wilson "the negro murderer," said he came from "bad stock," and followed the case to trial.

Only the Chicago Daily Tribune reported the mob, in a four-line Atlanta special headed "Saved from Lynching" that still called Wilson "the Macon murderer." The Georgia reports of his transfer spoke only of "safe keeping," leaving the mob unmentioned in the local press found.

Accounts differ on where Wilson was taken: the early items and the Chicago dispatch said near the Florida line, while the fuller Telegraph account named Apalachicola. Whether the shooting was self-defense was argued by both sides into the trial.

framing.detail: The Macon reward wire ran nationally, under heads such as 'Negro Murderer at Large', calling Wilson the man 'who murdered' the victim.
The Chicago Tribune ran the mob report in four lines headed 'Saved from Lynching', calling Wilson 'the Macon murderer'.
Georgia items via the Savannah Morning News called Wilson 'the negro murderer' from 'bad stock', urged his speedy capture, and spoke of 'safe keeping' but did not mention a mob.
